title: Composite: silicon sense chiplets mass-transferred onto glass DRAM panels
idea: TRIZ #40 Composite: large glass panels carry stacked oxide-TFT DRAM tiers, while all precision sensing lives in 50x50 um silicon sense chiplets placed every few millimetres by micro-LED-style mass transfer (millions per hour) and wired by panel redistribution layers; glass does storage, silicon does amplification.
why: 100x path: panel processing costs ~$100-300/m2 versus ~$100k/m2 for EUV DRAM wafers, so with ~0.3 um panel nanoimprint and 16-32 TFT tiers it aims at ~$0.1-0.5/GB; trade-offs: bulky modules, ~us latency and higher energy. Speculative because panel lithography must improve ~5x. Attacks Facts 4 and 7.
note: Multi-tier oxide-TFT DRAM on cheap glass with silicon sense chiplets could hit >10x cost/bit; panel lithography, overlay, us latency doubtful.

title: Photomultiplier dynodes: electron-multiplying gain register on every bitline
idea: Forced connection to a photomultiplier/EMCCD dynode chain: between cell and sense amp insert a short serial register of 8-10 high-field transfer gates in the SA strip, each adding ~1.2x impact-ionization gain, so a 1 fF cell's ~3,000 signal electrons arrive at the latch as ~15,000-20,000. The register is clocked only during the sense phase.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1): 5-6x pre-latch gain lets Cs fall from ~5 fF to ~1 fF, cutting pillar AR from ~70:1 toward ~20:1 or making small-cap 3D tiers viable; risks are excess gain noise and the high clock voltage.
note: 5x pre-latch gain would ease the capacitor wall, but EMCCD gain needs high clock voltages and adds excess noise.

title: Row-granular decompressor in the sense-amp stripe, after IBM MXT
idea: Failure mined: IBM's MXT compressed main memory died on decompression latency and a costly controller far from the DRAM. Fix: put a wide, row-granular decompressor (zero-run coding plus 4-bit quantization tables for AI weights, KV caches and activations) right after the secondary sense amps. Its work overlaps the activation's tRCD and rows are stored compressed, so effective capacity multiplies with no added latency.
why: 10x effective density at the same cost for AI data: 4:1 quantization x ~2.5:1 sparsity and zero-run coding = ~10x usable capacity per bit cell. It also cuts data-movement energy (fact 5) ~10x per useful value, for ~3% of die area.

title: Predictive-coding memory link transmitting only prediction errors
idea: The visual cortex sends mostly prediction errors, not raw images. Identical lightweight predictors (last-value, stride, zero-run) sit at both ends of a CXL/DIMM link on FPGA, and only the entropy-coded XOR residual crosses the wire. FPGA prototype, ~$600k in 18 months.
why: Fact 5: residuals are mostly zeros, so ~1.5-2x fewer bits cross a 10-20 pJ/bit link. That buys effective bandwidth and energy and lets fewer channels feed the same compute.

title: Partial-charge sip read makes DRAM sensing non-destructive
idea: A tightly controlled subthreshold wordline pulse lets only ~3% of the cell charge (~450 e-) leak into a 0.2 fF local sense node; kT/C charge noise there is ~6 e-, so 450 e- is a >20 sigma signal (~0.36 V). The cell keeps 97% of its charge, so nothing is restored and only the addressed 64 B is sensed; normal refresh tops cells up.
why: Kills destructive read and 128x overfetch (fact 8): per-useful-bit read energy from ~5.9 pJ toward ~0.1-0.3 pJ; also removes row-activation hammer stress.
note: Subthreshold partial read gives non-destructive 64B access; needs ~0.2 fF local sense nodes and precise sip control across Vt spread.

title: Open array-to-periphery bond standard for merchant cell wafers
idea: Inverting 'one company makes the whole DRAM die': publish an open hybrid-bond interface (bitline pitch, preamp spec, power and test pads) so array fabs sell bare cell wafers and many periphery designers, including US logic foundries, sell sense/decode dies, like UCIe for memory internals.
why: Splits the $15B integrated fab into an array-only fab plus commodity logic, lowering capital intensity and entry barriers; the US can take periphery share immediately.
note: Disaggregates array and periphery fabs; doubt: bitline-pitch bonding needs tight co-design, hard to commoditize.

title: Potluck cookbook: open-source, silicon-proven DRAM periphery IP commons
idea: A potluck works because everyone shares recipes. Fund an open-source library of DRAM periphery blocks (sense amps with offset calibration, row-hammer trackers, pumps, LPDDR/DDR5 PHYs) with silicon-proven layouts on U.S. 28/22 nm processes, so startups and foundries can build memory dies without decades of trade-secret circuit know-how.
why: Capital and U.S. manufacturability: periphery know-how is a hidden entry barrier; shared IP could cut a new entrant's design cost from ~$500M to ~$50-100M and save ~2 years.

title: Moth-ear minimal-periphery eDRAM compiler for open U.S. PDKs
idea: Noctuid moths detect bats with ears of just two neurons. An open-source compiler for SkyWater 130/GF180 generates 3T gain-cell eDRAM macros with radically minimal periphery: single-ended inverter sensing, shared counter refresh and standard-cell decoders. Two shuttles validate it for ~$700k in 24 months.
why: U.S. manufacturability: gives domestic mature-node fabs a working-memory macro ~2-3x denser than SRAM for chiplets now, seeding a U.S. DRAM design base.
note: Open gain-cell eDRAM compiler on U.S. PDKs; academic precedents exist.

title: Zettacore redox molecules: eight built-in reference levels per cell
idea: Failure mined: Zettacore's porphyrin molecular memory stored charge in discrete oxidation states but died on CMOS process heat and slow voltammetric reads. Fix: after the 400 C steps, graft thermally robust ferrocene/porphyrin mixtures with 7 redox couples onto a nanoporous TiN electrode. The sense amp's reference ladder is a reference electrode coated with the same molecules, so the potential plateaus self-calibrate and each cell stores 3 bits.
why: 10x at the same cost: 3 bits per cell x a crosspoint-compatible 4F^2 footprint (the porous electrode supplies ~50 fF-equivalent charge) x fewer reference generators = ~9-12x vs 1 bit per 6F^2. The molecules cost pennies per wafer.
note: Multi-redox molecules self-calibrate 3-bit levels; thermal budget, kinetics and endurance are major doubts.

title: Clonal-selection retention profiler RTL for commodity DDR5 on FPGA
idea: Like adaptive immunity, an FPGA controller (DRAM Bender-class) 'challenges' rows with stretched refresh and worst-case patterns. Failing rows are clonally expanded into a Bloom-filter list kept at 64 ms, and negative selection re-tests them to purge false positives and catch VRT drift. Everything else refreshes at 256 ms. Three engineers for 24 months plus $80k of boards, ~$900k total, produce licensable controller RTL.
why: Fact 3: ~4x fewer refreshes for >99.9% of rows saves ~70% of refresh energy and most of the 10-20% bandwidth tax, with no DRAM die change.
note: Close to RAIDR/REAPER/AVATAR prior art; value is licensable RTL, not new mechanism.

title: Rescue rejected DRAM dies behind a strong-ECC buffer controller
idea: Box: existing dies x existing access x existing SA x ECC buffer chip on module x existing substrate x existing fabs. Buy dies that fail JEDEC bins with <=1% bad bits at scrap prices and package them on modules or CXL cards whose buffer chip runs LDPC plus remapping, sold as a new grade.
why: Usable supply rises right away (recapturing yield loss of a few to 10%) with zero new fabs; cost per bit down.

title: Core-memory sense weaving cancels sneak current in selectorless 3D crosspoint
idea: Failure mined: core memory's sense wire zig-zagged through the cores so half-select noise cancelled, a trick lost in the move to semiconductors, while selectorless vertical crosspoints died on sneak current. Fix: pair each data pillar with a woven twin pillar that crosses the same word planes, with its half-selected cells biased in mirror image. A differential sense amp subtracts the matched sneak currents and leaves only the selected cell's current.
why: 10x at the same cost: without a selector, 32 deposited word planes stack under one pillar etch (4F^2 per tier, roughly 1.5 tiers' worth of patterning cost), ~10-20x bits/mm^2. The twin pillar doubles pillar count, not cost.
note: Sneak currents depend on stored data in both pillars, so mirror cancellation needs matched data; element endurance not DRAM-class.
